pages.text:
## we are better when we work together
Adam is running for Senate because he believes we need to stop the chaos and corruption in Washington by actually listening, and bringing people together to solve problems. He isn’t a career politician; he’s a Kansan who believes we are better when we work together.
## Meet Adam
Adam Hamilton is a Democratic candidate for the United States Senate in Kansas who has devoted his life to service. A fifth-generation Kansan, his family came to Dickinson County 147 years ago and helped build the towns of Hope and Elmo. His mother’s parents came to Wichita to work at Beechcraft, and his grandfather went on to fly for TWA.
Adam grew up in Prairie Village and married his high school sweetheart, LaVon, the week after graduation. They celebrated their 44th anniversary this June. They have two daughters, a granddaughter, and two dogs.
In 1990, at 25 years old, Adam and LaVon started a church in the Kansas City area with four people in a borrowed space. For 36 years he has served as pastor of a congregation roughly equal parts Republicans, Democrats and independents, doing the work to bring people together that politicians only talk about.The congregation he built has come together to give hundreds of thousands of volunteer hours and raise tens of millions of dollars to support neighbors and communities in need.
They became the largest source of donated food in Kansas City after the regional food bank and the area’s largest sponsor of blood drives. They gave away thousands of beds to children who didn’t have one, funded a mobile dental clinic that treats 2,700 kids a year at their schools, and invested millions of dollars in the lowest-income elementary schools in the area.
Adam is running for Senate because he believes we need to stop the chaos and corruption in Washington by actually listening to people and working together to get things done for Kansas families. Before deciding to run, he went on a listening tour, visiting communities all across the state to hear from people about their concerns. In his work, his writing, and now his campaign, Adam believes we are all called to serve our communities.
## Why Adam is Running for Senate
Adam’s running because Washington isn’t listening to us, and they’re making life harder for Kansans. Tariffs, foreign wars, and erratic leadership have made the basic necessities like food, medicine, and gas more expensive. While traveling around the state, Adam has heard from farmers, ranchers, and small-business owners who are struggling with rising costs for fuel and other inputs, and soaring health care costs.
## Kansans are asking for help, but folks in DC aren’t listening. That’s why his campaign is focused on:
- Listening to Kansans: Serving Kansans and listening to their concerns
- Solving the Affordability and Opportunity Crisis: Addressing the high costs of food, energy, and healthcare that are straining Kansas families.
- Building Bridges: Bringing common-sense back to Washington by working with Democrats, Republicans, and Independents to find solutions that put Kansans first.
- Restoring Decency and Humanity in Government: Rekindling faith in the American Dream by centering our politics on decency and our shared humanity.
Adam believes that Washington shouldn’t be the world’s bully or a place of gridlock, but a functional government that listens to the people it represents. He isn’t a career politician; he’s a Kansan who believes we are better when we work together.

## Adam’s Affordability Agenda
Protecting Kansas Families from Rising Energy Bills
Electricity prices have increased more sharply in the past year than they have in decades. Gas prices have surged. Yet Congress has failed to act to bring costs down for Kansas families, and the White House has made things worse. We need a comprehensive, all of the above strategy that creates jobs and increases energy independence while bringing down costs for consumers today.
- End self-destructive tariffs and unnecessary wars , which are driving up energy costs and hurting our ability to add energy capacity. Washington has repeatedly taken actions that directly increase costs and reduce affordability for Kansas families. When Washington imposes sweeping tariff taxes without a vote, the bill lands on Kansas farmers, manufacturers, and families in the form of higher prices on everything from equipment and fertilizer to groceries. The Constitution gives Congress responsibility over trade, and Congress should use it. Adam would prevent future administrations from harming Kansans by requiring congressional approval for new tariffs, and to publish the real cost to American families before those tariffs take effect. This is not a partisan idea. Kansas’s own Senator Jerry Moran has joined a bipartisan bill, the Trade Review Act, led by Republican Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell of Washington, to require exactly that.
- Require data centers to pay their fair share of electricity costs. Power usage by Data centers, driven by the rapid growth of AI, is growing rapidly throughout the United States, including rural states like Kansas. While these developments can provide economic benefits and jobs to areas that need them, we need to ensure that the companies behind them cover their costs instead of burdening ratepayers and earn the support of the towns and counties they move into. Republicans and Democrats agree on this. But where some support voluntary pledges, Adam would propose binding rules and legislation.
- Stop the war on domestic energy projects and restore energy production tax credits that increase our energy independence and create good-paying jobs. Adam supports all of the above energy production and believes Kansans should decide what happens on their land. More than two dozen Republican members of Congress asked to protect these credits before they were repealed, threatening nearly 10,000 jobs and shrinking the state’s economy by over $1 billion.
- Require competitive bidding processes for transmission projects instead of handing utility companies lucrative contracts at taxpayer expense. When a nearly half-billion-dollar transmission project is handed to a single utility with no competitive bidding, Kansas ratepayers can end up paying far more than they should. Competitive bidding has been shown to cut these costs by twenty to thirty percent. Politicians on both sides of the aisle should speak out against harmful policies that avoid competitive bidding, like the $493 million project that was handed to Evergy.
Protecting the Security Kansas Seniors Have Earned
In Kansas and across the country, millions of seniors are struggling to keep up with rising health care and everyday costs. Almost 20% of Kansans are 65 or older, and many live in rural communities where getting care can mean long drives, fewer providers, and harder choices. After a lifetime of work, Kansas seniors should be able to count on affordable care, stable benefits, and the chance to age with dignity. We need to protect social security and provide real solutions for seniors.
- Prioritize home-based care reimbursement to give seniors the option of aging at home instead of in a nursing facility or hospital. At-home care costs a fraction of care in a facility, and is often a better solution for seniors regardless of cost. We should make it financially and logistically feasible for seniors to access the care they need while aging in place with dignity, including by increasing reimbursement rates for home health aides and in-home care services.
- Expand Medicare to cover vision and dental so seniors are no longer forced to dig into their savings or skip care entirely because of holes in their coverage. Medicare excludes most dental and vision care, leaving seniors to pay hundreds to thousands of dollars a year out of pocket. Untreated dental disease is linked to diabetes and heart disease while vision loss increasing isolation and raises the risk of falls. We can close these gaps, keep seniors healthier, and save money down the line.
- Protect seniors from higher prices fueled by tariffs . Tariffs act as a hidden tax that ends up baked into the price of groceries, medications, utilities, and household goods — an estimated $1,700 a year for the average household — and they fall hardest on seniors getting by on a fixed Social Security check that doesn’t rise when those prices do. Requiring congressional approval before new tariffs take effect — like the Constitution requires — and publishing what those tariffs will cost families before they’re enacted, would protect the Kansans least able to bear them.
- Do more to fight elder fraud and scams . Fraud against seniors is surging — the FBI logged nearly $5 billion in losses in 2024, a 46% jump in complaints — and AI is making it far worse: with just a few seconds of audio scraped from social media, a scammer can clone a grandchild’s or spouse’s voice for a fake “family emergency” call. Rural seniors who bank and shop by phone are especially hard for local law enforcement to protect. Adam would strengthen the Department of Justice’s Elder Justice Initiative and give investigators the resources to pursue these cases — building on bipartisan work, including legislation Senator Marshall has sponsored to protect seniors from scams.
Housing Kansans Can Afford
Adam is a fifth-generation Kansan who grew up in Prairie Village, and he has seen firsthand how housing costs have gone up and up, all across the state.Home prices across the country have skyrocketed since the pandemic, and Kansas is no exception. In the nine years Roger Marshall has been in Washington, the average home price in the Kansas City area has risen by roughly eighty percent, the share of first-time buyers nationwide has fallen to a record low, and the typical first-time buyer is now forty years old. We can and must do better. Congress should make it easier to buy a home and easier to build one.
- The same across-the-board tariffs raising prices at the store are driving up the cost of building a new home by thousands of dollars and resulting in hundreds of thousands of new homes not being built. We must end these disastrous tariffs and require congressional approval for any future ones to bring building costs back down
- Modernize and standardize regulations for modular homes in order to increase the housing supply and provide more affordable options for families. Outdated regulations have slowed our ability to scale up their use nationwide, but by changing these rules we can increase the adoption of modular home building and bring down the cost at the same time. The Bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act has started this process, but we must go farther than reviewing financing barriers and commissioning studies on building codes. We need to do more than pass laws, we need to make sure the ones we have are enforced.
- Ban Wall St. and other investors from buying up single family homes and driving up prices on Kansas families. Investors increasingly are purchasing a large share of single family homes for sale nationwide, topping 30% of all sales in 2025. In 2025, roughly one in five homes sold in the Kansas City area went to an investor, among the highest rates of any major metro in the country, and across Kansas investors bought close to the same share. Congress just passed a first-ever limit on the largest institutional investors, and that is real progress. But the limit only applies going forward, does nothing about the homes already bought up, and leaves loopholes that let the biggest firms split into smaller entities to keep buying. Adam supports closing those loopholes so the rule actually protects Kansas families.
- Create tax credits for first time home buyers, firefighters, police officers, and teachers. Last year, the share of first-time home buyers dropped to just 21%, an all-time low, while the average age of first-time buyers rose all the way to 40 years old, also a record. Republicans and Democrats alike have supported the use of tax incentives to help first time home buyers. By creating new tax credits for young families looking to buy a home for the first time – as well as public servants like firefighters, police officers, and teachers – we can open up the dream of home ownership to more Kansas who have been priced out of the market.
- Stop anticompetitive price collusion from landlords, including the use of algorithmic pricing designed specifically to reduce competition and drive up rent for tenants.
Adam's Agenda to Lower Health Care Costs
Nearly 80% of Kansans are worried about being able to afford health care in the future, and nearly three-quarters say they skipped care in the past year because of the cost. At the same time, the country wastes billions of dollars every year on overpriced drugs and wasteful paperwork that helps no patient. We can do better on both fronts — these reforms lower costs for Kansas families while saving taxpayers money.
- Expand Medicare drug price negotiation and extend the savings to private insurance . Letting Medicare negotiate the price of high-cost prescription drugs — which it began doing for the first time under the 2022 law that also capped insulin at $35 a month and seniors’ out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000 — is projected to save Part D enrollees an estimated $1.5 billion in out-of-pocket costs in 2026 alone, with far more to come as more drugs are added. More than 571,000 Kansans rely on Medicare, but negotiation currently reaches only a short, slow-growing list of drugs and does nothing for the working-age Kansans on private insurance. Adam would expand the number of negotiated drugs, speed up the timeline, and extend negotiated prices to private plans — an approach CBO once estimated could save roughly $456 billion over a decade — while capping out-of-pocket drug costs at a reasonable level.
- Reverse the cuts to Medicaid and restore the ACA subsidies that hold premiums down. Two changes are raising health care costs for Kansas families at the same time. Kansas families are being squeezed from both sides. Deep federal Medicaid cuts are projected to drain up to $3.77 billion from KanCare and cost about 13,000 Kansans their coverage over the next decade. That would fall hardest on rural hospitals, and Kansas already has more hospitals at immediate risk of closing than any other state. At the same time, the end of enhanced ACA premium tax credits has made a typical subsidized Kansan’s monthly premium jump by more than half for 2026 — the steepest increase since the marketplace began. Because Kansas never expanded Medicaid, about 28,000 working Kansans are already stuck in the coverage gap: too well-off for KanCare, too poor for marketplace help.
- Cut waste, fraud, and abuse in Medicare without touching anyone’s benefits. Medicare often pays about 2.5 times more for the same outpatient service in a hospital than in a doctor’s office — so paying one fair rate regardless of where care is delivered (“site-neutral”) could save more than $150 billion over a decade. Private Medicare Advantage plans, meanwhile, are projected to be overpaid by roughly $76 billion in 2026 because they document members as sicker than they really are. These are real opportunities for Republicans and Democrats to save billions in taxpayer dollars. Adam would go after both problems, and he would reform prior authorization so insurance paperwork cannot delay or deny care that doctors say patients need. This should be common ground.
- Protect and invest in rural hospitals . Kansas has more rural hospitals at immediate risk of closing than any other state — roughly two-thirds are at risk overall — largely because insurers, including Medicare Advantage, don’t pay enough to cover the cost of care. A rural hospital is often a county’s largest employer and its only nearby emergency room, and studies find that closing one raises deaths from time-sensitive emergencies like heart attacks and strokes by about 10%. The squeeze is sharpest in childbirth, where only about a third of rural Kansas hospitals still deliver babies. Reversing the Medicaid cuts would help, but Adam would go further to fix the underpayment and keep these hospitals’ doors open.
- Reform medical billing and medical debt . In 2024, more than a third of U.S. households carried medical debt, and 43% of Kansans report a financial burden from medical bills — made worse by high interest and aggressive collection. In 45 states, including Kansas, a collector can garnish a patient’s wages and even jail them over unpaid medical bills. Adam would cap interest on medical debt, limit wage garnishment, and keep medical debt off credit reports — reforms a growing number of states have already adopted with no disruption to hospitals or care. Much of this debt is disputed or billed in error in the first place, sweeping people who never owed the money into collections.
- Protect a woman’s right to choose and prevent further government interference into personal decisions by codifying the access to contraception into law. Require insurers to cover non-prescription over the counter birth control just like they cover prescription contraception.
Support Kansas Agriculture, Producers, and Consumers
It’s been a generation since Kansas families felt so much pain at the grocery store. Global instability is hurting Kansas, but so have many of our own government’s choices — the war in Iran, the trade war, a farm bill three years late, and an inadequate response to animal-health crises like Avian Influenza and the New World Screwworm. Leaders have failed Kansans and Kansas farmers in their most basic responsibility: a secure and affordable food supply.
Protect Kansas farmers from tariffs and expand export markets for Kansas products. Farmers in Kansas are being hit hard from all sides –hundreds of farms closed last year, in large part because tariffs drove up the cost of equipment and hurt exports of Kansas products. We should immediately get rid of tariffs that are hurting our farmers’ ability to make a living,double funding for USDA’s export promotion programs – an investment economists project would generate more than $44 billion in new agricultural exports, much of it Kansas wheat, sorghum, and beef. And Congress should re-engage in trade policy and push for new market access agreements.
Fund an overwhelming response to the animal disease outbreaks driving up the price of eggs and beef. Avian influenza cost American consumers $14.5 billion in higher egg prices in a single year, and with the New World Screwworm now detected in cattle in Texas, beef prices – already forecast to rise 12% this year – are at risk of climbing even higher. Congress must fully fund the animal disease vaccine bank , laboratory network, and preparedness programs; accelerate the new domestic sterile-fly production facility; and pass the bipartisan Rural Veterinary Workforce Act so rural Kansas can recruit large-animal vets.
Finally pass the full farm bill after three years of Congressional delay. The 2018 farm bill expired in 2023, and Kansas farmers have been operating on extensions and uncertainty ever since. The House finally passed its version in April, but the Senate hasn’t acted and the current extension runs out September 30. Congress needs to finish the job and give agriculture five years of certainty .
Give agriculture the stable, legal workforce it needs to keep food affordable. Labor shortages on cow-calf operations, farms, and dairies drive up the cost of producing food, and those costs land on Kansas families at the checkout line. Congress must reform the broken H-2A guest-worker program — permitting year-round visas that reflect modern needs, lowering compliance costs, and giving existing workers a path to legal status .
Make fertilizer in America . The wars with Iran and in Ukraine caused huge increases in fertilizer costs, and those costs land directly on grocery shelves. USDA’s Fertilizer Production Expansion Program has already invested in dozens of facilities — including in Kansas — and is being expanded with accelerated permitting. Congress should supercharge it .
Cut prices at the pump with year-round E15 . Homegrown ethanol blends save drivers 20 to 40 cents per gallon while building new markets for Kansas corn and sorghum. The House passed year-round E15 legislation in May with bipartisan support — the Senate should send it to the President’s desk .
Ban algorithmic price-fixing at grocery stores that takes advantage of consumers and reduces competition. Dynamic pricing, in which grocery chains change prices based on market conditions and even shoppers’ personal information, is becoming more and more widespread. We need to prohibit the practice and penalize retailers that take advantage of consumers.
End the policy chaos in Washington that drives economic uncertainty and volatile prices — beginning by lowering the partisan temperature, bringing Republicans and Democrats together, and showing a unified face to a global economy that looks to America for leadership.
Ending the Chaos and Corruption In Washington
Washington has become overrun by chaos and corruption, with far too many politicians on both sides of the aisle putting themselves and special interests first instead of listening to their constituents’ needs. It’s time for a change. From rampant conflicts of interest and self-dealing to a broken campaign finance and electoral system, Kansans deserve leaders who truly believe in government ethics and real accountability.
Ending Conflicts of Interest
- Prohibit members of Congress and their households from buying or selling individual stocks while in office. We send politicians to Congress to represent us and our values, not to enrich themselves – but in one three year period, more than a third of them reported stock trades, and nearly one in five sat on congressional committees that may have given them insider information. The potential conflicts of interest aren’t just hypothetical – our elected officials have even sold stock in Medicaid providers just a week before voting for Medicaid cuts. It is time we ended the practice by requiring members to place all individual stocks, bonds, commodities, cryptocurrencies, and investment assets into a qualified blind trust or divest completely.
- Extend the stock trading ban to cover cryptocurrency and digital assets . While trading crypto and other digital assets may be less common than stock trading, it is still ripe for abuse by lawmakers seeking to profit from their roles in government.
- Prohibit members and their staff from gambling on prediction markets , which can create direct financial incentives for elected official around specific legislative outcomes. While the Senate recently passed a resolution to that effect, Congress should still enact legislation banning the practice for good.
- Pass a constitutional amendment establishing term limits for members of Congress in the U.S. House of Representatives, U.S. Senate, and the Supreme Court. The longer elected officials remain in Washington, the more entrenched and cozier with special interests and lobbyists they become – no matter which side of the aisle they serve on. Establishing 18-year term limits would be one of the most effective, and efficient, ways we could remake, and eventually fix, a broken Congress.
- Establish age limits for members of Congress and for members of the Supreme Court. While some elected officials are able to operate at a high level in their later years, we all suffer when politicians remain in office beyond their ability to adequately serve their constituents.
- Strengthen residency requirements for members of Congress to ensure that our elected officials actually live alongside the people they represent, and don’t just happen to own real estate in the area. Too many lawmakers are completely disconnected from their constituents, particularly those who become entrenched in D.C. for decades.
- Put an end to billionaires and special interests flooding our elections with dark money. In the 2024 election alone, more than $1 billion in dark money expenditures were made. This money is drowning out the voices of normal voters and causing our elected officials to become even more beholden to special interests.
- Hold Congress accountable by withholding member pay during government shutdowns . When everyday Americans don’t do their jobs, they aren’t paid. Members of Congress must face the same real-world consequences: if they don’t pass a budget in time, they don’t receive a salary until the government reopens. No budget, no pay.
- Extend the lobbying ban for members of Congress and their senior staff. U.S. Senators of prohibited from becoming federal lobbyists for just two years after leaving office, while Representatives only have to wait one year. It is no surprise, then, that so many cash in on lucrative lobbying gigs soon after leaving office – at our expense. We need to permanently prohibit members of Congress from becoming federal lobbyists; and extend the one-year “cooling off” period for senior staff.
- Restore protections for Inspectors General in order to prevent political interference in the work of independent watchdogs. Inspectors general exist to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse across government, and to ensure government agencies work for the people, not for special interests or one political party. We must ensure that independent IGs are qualified and able to remain independent, and that they cannot be removed without cause or congressional notice.
- Limit presidential pardon power. No president should be able to put themselves, their family, or their allies above the law. We need to root out corrupt uses of clemency power and punish wrongdoers who try to buy pardons from presidents.
Strengthening Consumer Protections and Supporting Small Business
Successful businesses and entrepreneurs are key to Kansas’s success, but corporations should not be allowed to take advantage of hardworking families and taxpayers to boost profits while driving up the cost of living.
- Ban junk fees that companies hide from consumers across industries like lodging, ticketing, telecommunications, travel, and more. What you see should be what you pay, with no surprise at checkout.
- Restore overdraft fee protections to prevent banks from aggressively profiting off consumers. The CFPB’s 2024 rule would save households billions a year, but Senator Marshall celebrated his vote to repeal it.
- Investigate private equity consolidation in essential sectors including health care, housing, and groceries. These anticompetitive roll-ups drive up costs for ordinary Kansans. In May 2024 the FTC and DOJ opened a joint inquiry into “serial acquisitions” and roll-up strategies that buy up many small competitors through deals each too small to trigger antitrust review. The harm shows up in in places Kansans cannot avoid like the hospital, your rental home, the nursing home, and the grocery store.
- Hold big corporations accountable by requiring clawback provisions for economic-development incentives, so taxpayer dollars come with guarantees that companies deliver the jobs and investment they promised.
Standing with Kansas Workers
Kansans understand hard work, but workers’ ability to get ahead is under pressure from anti-labor legislation to wage theft to the rise of AI in the workplace.
- Restore equity between workers and employers by strengthening the right to organize and eliminating corporate loopholes, starting with the bipartisan Faster Labor Contracts Act to speed first-contract negotiations. Workers who win a union election routinely wait a year or more for a first contract because the employer stalls. The Bipartisan Faster Labor Contracts Act would require an employer to begin bargaining within 10 days after workers vote to unionize, with mediation and arbitration backstops if no first contract is reached.
- Fully fund National Labor Relations Board, OSHA, and NIOSH so the agencies that protect workers’ rights and safety can actually do their jobs. These are the cops on the beat for workplace safety and labor law and they have been running on fumes.
- Crack down on wage theft — unpaid overtime, minimum-wage violations, illegal deductions, and stolen tips — through harsher penalties and stronger Department of Labor enforcement. Wage theft drains billions from working people’s paychecks every year, and lack of enforcement means most of it is never caught.
- Protect workers from AI-only employment decisions without human oversight. The No Robot Bosses Act would require real human review of hiring, firing, and promotions.

## Kansas is the number one Senate race in the country
Election experts like Nate Silver are calling the Kansas Senate race a TOSS UP!
All eyes are on Kansas – and my opponent is panicking. That’s why he and his super PAC allies are spending millions of dollars on attack ads against me. With more voters casting their ballots every day, we have to fight back before it’s too late. Please, will you chip in whatever you can spare to help me flip this seat and bring Kansas values to Washington?
